proposals.observation: The Daily Blog Post workflow failed at 06:41 on 3 July. The content queue shows only 1 post queued against 47 published, so the pipeline is the bottleneck, not the idea bank. With one post queued, a second consecutive failure tomorrow empties the queue entirely and breaks the publishing streak. The Funnel-Hack Digest also failed the same morning, suggesting either a shared dependency (API key, Node version, scheduled-job concurrency) or a time-window collision between the two workflows.
proposals.proposal: Inspect the Daily Blog Post workflow logs for the failure reason before the next scheduled run. The most common causes given the Funnel-Hack Digest also failed in the same window: a shared secret (OPENAI_API_KEY or MAILERLITE_API_KEY) expired or was rotated without updating both workflow files, or both workflows fired simultaneously and hit a rate limit. The fix is a single-file edit to the workflow YAML: either stagger the cron schedule by 30 minutes, add a retry step, or update the secret reference. Because .github/workflows/* is blocked from Fred's direct edits, this proposal is flagged for Joel to action manually. The file path and diff shape are described precisely below so the edit takes under five minutes.

proposals.impact: reduces intro-load abandonment by giving visitors a reason to start
proposals.observation: In 48 hours, the quiz recorded 2 sessions and 0 starts. Both visitors loaded the intro screen and left without pressing anything. The furthest_step_distribution shows intro_load: 2 and nothing beyond that. Both arrivals were direct traffic, meaning these are likely warm visitors (bookmarked, returning, or sent a link) who still could not find a reason to begin. The problem is almost certainly the intro copy or button, not awareness.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the quiz intro's headline and sub-text to name the specific cost of not starting, grounded in the lived moment Joel's ICP recognises. The current copy (reproduced below from the file) is generic enough that any financial coach could have written it. Replace it with something only Joel could write, rooted in the gym-bag-and-unopened-tab moment: the feeling of earning well, looking competent, and quietly knowing the savings account tells a different story. The call-to-action button text also needs to shift from a vague invitation to a grounded, specific commitment.

Find out what's actually driving your money decisions

You earn a reasonable amount. You know the basics. And yet the account balance at month-end never quite reflects any of that. This 3-minute quiz identifies the specific pattern underneath — the one that keeps reasserting itself no matter how many spreadsheets you've built.

proposals.impact: lifts 37.5% open rate toward the 66% benchmark set by Money Vigilance sequence
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation achieves a 66.67% open rate on 12 sends. The Money Worship automation sits at 37.5% on 16 sends, the lowest of the three active sequences. Both sequences serve people who have completed the same quiz, so list quality is comparable. The gap of 29 percentage points is too large to attribute to audience size alone. The most probable cause is the subject line or preview text on Money Worship email 01, which sets the open trajectory for the whole sequence.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the subject line and preview text of Money Worship email 01. The current subject line (reproduced below) frames money worship as a concept to learn about, which keeps the reader at an intellectual distance. The Money Vigilance sequence likely opens better because vigilance feels personally charged: people recognise it as a thing they do to themselves. The Money Worship subject line needs to put the reader inside the moment of the behaviour, not above it.
